title: Safety & Redundancy: Designing for What Happens When It Fails
oneLiner: Industrial control treats "what happens when this fails" as a first-class design question -- not an edge case to handle later, but a property every output and every controller is designed around from the start.
keyTakeaway: "Fail-safe" doesn't mean a device's normal state is OFF -- it means the device is specifically DESIGNED so that losing power (or losing signal, or losing communication) puts it into whichever physical state is actually safe for THAT device, which is sometimes "stopped" (a conveyor motor needs power to run) and sometimes "engaged" (a spring-applied brake clamps on when its coil loses power and needs power to release). Both are de-energize-to-safe: power OFF is the safe state, even though the safe mechanical state is different.
explanation:
A general application crashing usually just means downtime -- annoying, costly, but rarely dangerous. A PLC controlling physical machinery losing power, losing its program, or losing communication can mean a very different kind of failure: a motor that doesn't stop, a valve that doesn't close, a press that doesn't retract. FAIL-SAFE design is the discipline of choosing, for every single output, which physical state is actually safe, and then wiring/programming that device so power loss (or any other fault) naturally lands it there -- not by adding extra code to detect and handle the failure, but because the hardware itself defaults there when nothing is driving it.

This is why some devices are "energize to run" (a conveyor motor -- no power means no rotation, which is the safe state) while others are "energize to RELEASE" (a fail-safe brake -- it's spring-engaged by default and needs power specifically to release, so a power loss engages the brake instead of leaving a load free to fall). Same underlying idea -- power loss must be safe -- and in both cases power OFF is the safe state; what differs is what "safe" looks like mechanically: the motor stops, while the brake clamps ON. (The opposite design, energize-to-trip, does exist -- some fire-and-gas systems must be powered to act, such as a deluge valve driven open on a fire signal -- but because a broken wire or lost supply silently disables it, it's chosen deliberately and the circuit is continuously monitored for faults.)

REDUNDANCY asks the same question about the controller itself, but for a different goal: AVAILABILITY. High-availability systems often run a hot-standby PLC alongside the primary, continuously mirroring its state, ready to take over if the primary faults -- because the PLC controlling the process is otherwise a single point of failure that stops the whole process. The switchover is fast but not instant: it takes a bounded, vendor-specified time (often tens of milliseconds, which can be longer than a scan) and is only bumpless within the limits the vendor documents. That keeps the process RUNNING; it doesn't make it SAFE. Functions that protect people (emergency stops, guard interlocks, overpressure trips) still need an independent safety system -- a SIL-rated safety PLC or safety relays -- that works no matter what the redundant control PLCs are doing.
